name: AIGRCeler discovery profile
note: What DISCOVER asks about one AI system, in plain words. Each question names the risk scenarios and controls that use the answer.

sections.title: People who use it and people it affects

fields.label: what it does
fields.q: In one or two sentences, what does the system do, and who asked for it?
fields.why: Every later judgment (risk, controls, legal duties) is made against this purpose.

fields.label: who answers for it
fields.q: Who is the one person who answers for what this system does to customers and the business?
fields.why: Without a named owner nobody can be asked to fix a problem or accept a risk.

fields.label: other AI tools used around it
fields.q: Does anyone working on this process use other AI tools that are not on the company's list (free chatbots, browser add-ins, AI features inside software you already pay for)? Which ones, and what goes into them?
fields.why: Unlisted AI tools beside this system can leak data or change results without anyone governing them.

fields.label: lifecycle stage
fields.q: Where is it today: still an idea, a pilot, in everyday use, or being retired?
fields.why: A system already in use needs its controls sooner than one still being planned.

fields.label: technical owner
fields.q: Who looks after it technically from day to day (the person to call when it breaks)?
fields.why: Incidents and changes need a technical person who can act.

fields.label: intended use
fields.q: What specific uses is it meant for, and what must it never be used for?
fields.why: Use outside the intended purpose is a main source of harm and of legal exposure.

fields.label: in use since
fields.q: If it is already in use, since when, and how many people have used it so far?
fields.why: Time in use shows how much history (results, complaints) exists to learn from.

fields.label: business value
fields.q: What problem does it solve, and what happens to the business if it is switched off?
fields.why: How much the business depends on it sets how hard it is to stop it when something goes wrong.

fields.label: who uses it
fields.q: Who uses it (which roles or customers), and roughly how many people?
fields.why: Who uses it decides what training and oversight they need.

fields.label: how many people it reaches
fields.q: How many people use it or are affected by it? few = a handful, many = hundreds, very-many = thousands or more.
fields.why: Scale sets the tier: more people means a mistake costs more.

fields.label: who is affected by what it produces
fields.q: Who is affected by what it produces, even if they never see it (customers, job applicants, patients, staff, the public)?
fields.why: The people affected are who the risk assessment is really about.

fields.label: vulnerable groups
fields.q: Are children, patients, job seekers, employees, elderly people or people in financial difficulty among those affected? Say which, or say none.
fields.why: Groups with less power or protection are harmed more easily and are protected more strongly by law.

fields.label: user training
fields.q: What training do the people who use or review the system have?
fields.why: People who do not know its limits trust it too much or too little.

fields.label: affected consulted
fields.q: Have the people it affects, or their representatives, been asked for their views? How, and what changed because of it?
fields.why: Hearing from affected people finds harms the builders cannot see.

fields.label: societal effect
fields.q: Could it affect groups beyond its direct users (a community, a profession, the environment)?
fields.why: Wider effects need to be named before they can be weighed.

fields.label: whether it decides anything about a person
fields.q: Does it decide, rank, score or recommend anything about an identifiable person (hiring, credit, care, pricing, access, discipline)? Answer yes or no, and say what.
fields.why: Decisions about people carry the strongest fairness and legal duties and rule out the light lane.

fields.label: decisions made
fields.q: What exactly does it decide or recommend, and what happens next because of its output?
fields.why: The step after the output shows how much damage a wrong output can do.

fields.label: how much a person checks its output
fields.q: Is every output checked by a person before it is used (reviewed), only some outputs (sampled), or none (automated)?
fields.why: The less a person checks, the more the system itself must be trusted.

fields.label: whether a person can overrule it, and how often
fields.q: Can a person overrule it? Who, how, and how often do they actually do so?
fields.why: A review step that nobody uses to change anything is not oversight.

fields.label: whether it takes actions on its own
fields.q: Can it take actions with real effects on its own (send messages, change records, spend money, call other systems)? Answer yes or no, and say what.
fields.why: A system that acts, and not only advises, can cause harm at machine speed.

fields.label: whether its output reaches customers unchecked
fields.q: Does it write or send anything to customers or the public without a person checking it first? Answer yes or no.
fields.why: Unchecked output reaching the public is a reputational and legal risk and rules out the light lane.

fields.label: ai disclosure
fields.q: Are people told that they are dealing with AI, or that AI is used on their information? How?
fields.why: People have a right to know, and surprise damages trust.

fields.label: appeal path
fields.q: How can an affected person question a result, ask for a person to look again, or report a problem?
fields.why: Without a way to contest a result, errors about people stay uncorrected.

fields.label: what data it uses
fields.q: What data does it use (records, documents, prompts, files), and where does each kind come from?
fields.why: Poor or unknown data is the most common cause of poor results.

fields.label: whether the data is personal or sensitive
fields.q: Is any of the data about identifiable people (personal), or about health, beliefs, biometrics, ethnicity, children, finances or criminal records (sensitive)? none, personal or sensitive.
fields.why: Personal and sensitive data bring privacy duties and rule out the light lane.

fields.label: data origin
fields.q: Who owns the data, and are you allowed to use it for this? Is it your own records, customer-provided, bought, scraped, public or supplied by a vendor?
fields.why: Data used without the right to use it taints everything built on it.

fields.label: data basis
fields.q: What permission or reason does the company rely on to use personal data this way (consent, contract, legitimate interest), and were people told? Has counsel or your privacy officer confirmed it?
fields.why: A system built on personal data without a valid basis can be ordered to stop. This is a question for counsel, not for AIGRCeler to answer.

fields.label: data retention
fields.q: How long is the personal data kept, and can it be deleted when someone asks?
fields.why: Keeping data too long or being unable to delete it is a common finding.

fields.label: data flows out
fields.q: What company data leaves the company (to the vendor and its sub-suppliers), and to which countries?
fields.why: Data sent outside is out of your control and may cross borders.

fields.label: data quality
fields.q: How is the quality of the data checked, and is it checked that it fits the people the system affects?
fields.why: Data that does not represent the people affected produces unfair results.

fields.label: prompts logs
fields.q: Do prompts, logs or outputs contain personal or confidential information? Who can read them?
fields.why: Logs and prompts are a quiet place for data to leak.

fields.label: training data
fields.q: Was it trained or fine-tuned on company data? Is training data kept apart from test data and recorded for each version?
fields.why: You cannot explain or repeat a result without knowing what the model learned from.

fields.label: how it is sourced
fields.q: Did you build it, adapt someone else's model, buy a service, run an open-source model yourselves, or is it a feature inside a product you bought?
fields.why: How it was sourced decides which risks and controls apply.

fields.label: which vendor and model
fields.q: Which vendor, and which model or product name?
fields.why: You cannot check a vendor or follow its changes without knowing who it is.

fields.label: model version
fields.q: Which version is in use today, and how would you find out that it changed?
fields.why: A silent version change can break behaviour, and proof tied to an old version stops counting.

fields.label: whether it is generative AI
fields.q: Does it write text, images, code or speech (generative AI)? Answer yes or no.
fields.why: Generative systems can invent facts, leak data and be tricked by their inputs.

fields.label: technique
fields.q: What kind of AI is it (classifier, prediction, recommendation, language model, agent...)?
fields.why: The kind of AI decides how it fails and how it can be tested.

fields.label: hosting
fields.q: Where does it run (vendor cloud, your cloud, your own servers, a device), and in which country?
fields.why: Where it runs decides who can reach it and which country's rules touch the data.

fields.label: integrations tools
fields.q: Which tools, plug-ins or other systems can it call or read from, and with what permissions?
fields.why: Every connection is a way for a failure or an attack to spread.

fields.label: change process
fields.q: How is it changed or updated, by whom, how often, and how is a change tested before it goes live?
fields.why: Untested changes quietly break behaviour that was once checked.

fields.label: gpai
fields.q: Is it built on a general-purpose AI model from a provider (a large language model)? Which one, and what documentation does the provider give you about it?
fields.why: Providers of general-purpose models owe their customers documentation; you need it to judge your own risk.

fields.label: licences
fields.q: What licence or terms cover the model, the data and the outputs (including open-source and intellectual property)?
fields.why: Licence terms can limit use or make the company liable.

fields.label: resources
fields.q: What people, computing and budget does it take to run and oversee it? Who would take over if they left?
fields.why: A system nobody has time to oversee is unsupervised in practice.

fields.label: how anyone checks that it works well
fields.q: How does anyone check that it works well? What is measured, and who looks at the result?
fields.why: If nobody measures it, nobody will notice when it gets worse.

fields.label: known limits
fields.q: What are its known weaknesses, where does it fail, and what should it never be trusted for?
fields.why: Known limits must reach the people who rely on the system.

fields.label: test results
fields.q: What testing was done before it was used, and what were the results (accuracy, unusual inputs, fairness)?
fields.why: Results before launch are the baseline for every later check.

fields.label: bias testing
fields.q: Was it checked for uneven results across groups (gender, age, ethnicity, language, disability)? What was found?
fields.why: A system can be accurate on average and unfair to a group.

fields.label: monitoring now
fields.q: What is watched in live use (accuracy, drift, complaints, cost, errors), and who looks at it?
fields.why: Results drift as the world changes; only watching shows it.

fields.label: past problems
fields.q: Have there been errors, complaints, near-misses or incidents with it? What happened and what was done?
fields.why: Past problems are the best predictor of future ones.

fields.label: target level
fields.q: What level of accuracy or error is acceptable for this use, and who decided that?
fields.why: Without a stated target nobody can say whether it is good enough.

fields.label: explainability
fields.q: Can someone explain, in plain words, why it gave a particular result?
fields.why: People affected by a decision are entitled to understand it.

fields.label: adversarial testing
fields.q: Has anyone tried to trick, break or misuse it (red-teaming, prompt-injection tests, security testing)? What did they find?
fields.why: Systems that have never been attacked on purpose have unknown weaknesses.

fields.label: access control
fields.q: Who can use it, change it or see inside it (including its data and keys)? How is that access reviewed?
fields.why: Uncontrolled access lets the wrong person change or steal it.

fields.label: logging
fields.q: What records are kept of what it was asked and what it did, for how long, and who can read them?
fields.why: Without records you cannot show a regulator or a customer what happened.

fields.label: secrets keys
fields.q: Where are its passwords and service keys kept, and who can see them?
fields.why: Leaked keys give attackers the same access the system has.

fields.label: security review
fields.q: Has the code, the libraries, the running system or the vendor been security-tested or assessed? When, and what was found?
fields.why: Vulnerable software or a compromised component can undermine everything else.

fields.label: misuse paths
fields.q: How could someone misuse or attack it, and what stops them?
fields.why: Naming the attack paths is the start of defending them.

fields.label: what depends on what it produces
fields.q: What other systems, reports or decisions depend on what it produces? (Say 'nothing' if nothing does.)
fields.why: A failure spreads to everything that depends on it.

fields.label: upstream dependencies
fields.q: What does it depend on (data feeds, vendor services, other systems)?
fields.why: If an input fails or changes, the system's results change with it.

fields.label: fallback
fields.q: If it is wrong or down, what happens? Is there a manual way to carry on, and how long can the business cope without it?
fields.why: A system with no fallback cannot be switched off safely.

fields.label: whether it can affect safety
fields.q: Could a wrong result hurt someone's health or physical safety? Answer yes or no.
fields.why: Safety impact rules out the light lane and raises the minimum risk.

fields.label: how bad the worst outcome could be
fields.q: If it is wrong, how bad is the worst realistic outcome? minor = an annoyance, business = money or reputation, rights-or-safety = someone's rights, livelihood, health or safety.
fields.why: This is the main input to the tier.

fields.label: the worst realistic outcome
fields.q: Describe the worst realistic thing that could happen if it is wrong, who would be hurt, and whether it could be undone.
fields.why: A concrete worst case makes the likelihood and impact ratings honest.

fields.label: which countries its users are in
fields.q: In which countries or regions are the people it affects, and where does the company operate it?
fields.why: The countries decide which laws apply.

fields.label: whether it is used in a regulated field
fields.q: Is it used in a regulated field (banking, insurance, health, employment, education, public services)? Answer yes or no, and say which.
fields.why: Regulated sectors have their own rules and rule out the light lane.

fields.label: whether it touches the EU
fields.q: Does it affect people in the European Union, or is any of it run there? yes, no or not-sure.
fields.why: If it touches the EU, the EU AI Act may apply. Whether it does is a question for counsel.

fields.label: the company's role under the EU AI Act
fields.q: Under the EU AI Act, is the company the one that built it and puts it on the market (provider), only uses it (deployer), imports it, resells it, or is it not sure? provider, deployer, importer, distributor, authorised-representative, none or not-sure.
fields.why: The duties differ greatly by role. This is a question for counsel.

fields.label: the view on its EU AI Act class
fields.q: What is the company's current view of how the EU AI Act classifies this use, and has counsel been asked? prohibited-concern, high-risk, transparency-duty, minimal or not-sure.
fields.why: A prohibited or high-risk use needs legal steps before it can go live. This records a view; counsel decides.

fields.label: whether counsel has been asked
fields.q: Have legal counsel or your privacy officer been asked about this system? Which questions are still open with them?
fields.why: Legal questions only counsel can answer must not stay unasked.

fields.label: prior assessments
fields.q: Which impact or privacy assessments, audits or approvals already exist for it, and when were they done?
fields.why: Existing assessments save work and show what has already been judged.

fields.label: contracts
fields.q: Which contract or terms cover it (data processing, audit rights, security, liability, change notice)? Where are they?
fields.why: The contract decides who pays and who must act when something goes wrong.

fields.label: sector rules
fields.q: Which sector rules or regulator guidance do you know apply to it?
fields.why: Sector duties are easy to miss and are enforced separately.

fields.label: certifications
fields.q: Which standards or certifications does the company or the vendor hold or work towards (ISO 42001, ISO 27001, SOC 2...)?
fields.why: Certifications show what has been independently checked.

fields.label: oversight owner
fields.q: Who reviews its results day to day, and how much of their time does that take?
fields.why: A named reviewer with time is what makes oversight real.

fields.label: incident contact
fields.q: Who is called when it goes wrong, and who is the vendor's contact for an incident?
fields.why: In an incident every minute lost to finding the right person counts.

fields.label: existing policies
fields.q: Which existing company policies already cover it (acceptable use, data, security, procurement)?
fields.why: Existing policies are the base the AI controls build on.

fields.label: approval history
fields.q: Who approved it for use, when, and on what basis?
fields.why: A launch without a recorded approval cannot be defended afterwards.
